Exiled from History: Africa in Hegel’s Academic Practice
results.abstract: Abstract: Many scholars, African and otherwise, have excoriated G.W.F. Hegel for his dismissal of Africa from history and progress in his lectures on the philosophies of history and religion. This has been done by quoting his texts and setting his words in the context of his influence on nineteenth-century European imperialism and racism. A different approach informs this paper. I treat Hegel, a complicated person, as a working university academic with a career to make and an overriding desire to publicize his own thought. I provide biographical insights relevant to these matters, and go on to examine specific texts about Africa that Hegel either sought out or chanced upon, read, misread, excerpted, used, and misused in support of his theorizing and apriorism. Attention is paid throughout to the construction, recording, and dissemination of Hegel’s lectures, and to aspects of their reception and authority in the educational formation of selected modern African intellectuals. I argue that such persons and African studies more widely are still trying to come to grips with the long and enduring shadow cast by Hegel over both the past and present of the continent. Résumé: De nombreux chercheurs africains et d’ailleurs ont vertement critiqué G.W.F. Hegel pour son exclusion de l’Afrique tant de l’histoire que du progrès dans ses conférences sur les philosophies de l’histoire et de la religion. Cette critique a été faite en citant ses textes et en plaçant ses paroles dans le contexte de son influence sur l’impérialisme et le racisme européens du XIXe siècle. Une approche différente informe ce papier. Je traite Hegel, un personnage compliqué, comme un universitaire de métier devant construire sa carrière et désirant très fortement faire connaître sa pensée. Je fournis des éclairages biographiques pertinents sur ces questions et analyse ensuite des textes spécifiques sur l’Afrique que Hegel a soit recherchés ou trouvés par hasard, lus, mal lus, extraits de leur contexte, utilisés ou utilisés à mauvais escient pour soutenir ses théories et préjugés. Une attention toute particulière est accordée à la construction, à l’édition et à la diffusion des conférences de Hegel, ainsi qu’aux aspects de leur réception et de leur autorité dans la formation pédagogique de certains intellectuels africains contemporains. Je soutiens que ces personnes et les études africaines plus largement tentent encore de s’attaquer à l’influence très vaste et durable des idées développées par Hegel sur le passé et le présent du continent.

O pan-africanismo em Abdias do Nascimento e a proposta de descolonização
results.abstract: The importance of Jose Abdias do Nascimento for the formation of the Brazilian intelligentsia is an inspiration to the anti-racist struggle of the Brazilian black population. His intellectual production problematized the nuances of anti-black racism in Brazil and articulated forms of resistance to the erasure of Brazilian black-African history. Based on these theses we relate to Nkolo Foe's proposal for decolonization in opposition to the episthemicide directed at African philosophy. Thus, at first, the focus will be on the conception of Pan-Africanism through theorists such as Marcus Garvey and Kwame Nkrumah. Finally, to resume the Brazilian thinker through the theses present in Quilombismo to think together with the African philosophy of Nkolo Foe the political-philosophical resistance to anti-black racism.

results.abstract: In human history, there are too many wars, it is difficult to list fully. Entering the century XX-XXI, wars still continued at different scales. Besides, there is also the divisions of the nation, the disintegration of the social system ... Is it possible, the world will be divided and increasingly distant each other? So far, still no theory has answered that question. Perhaps the main reason is not found a theoretical basis, or a thinking model. As is known, in nature and human society, there are often common or similar laws. However, human society is a very complex system. Therefore, sociologists often take ideas from natural science as a scientific basis and research model. This method has been used by René Descartes, Herbert Spencer, Kenneth D. Bailey, Talcott Parson, Niklas Luhmann, Erich Jantsh, Peter Grimes... Although many natural models have been used for social research, none has shown the trend of social evolution. So, to find this model, we consider the evolutionary trend of nature. The result showed, in the scale of the universe, matter has evolved in convergent trend. Thanks to that trend, the first stars are formed, followed by galaxies, black holes and the heavy chemical elements ... The convergent trends also exist in the water environment on Earth and lead to life formation. In biosystem, the biochemical molecules: DNA, protein, collagen, reserve lipid...also tend to increase a convergent level in biological evolution. The convergent trend in material evolution is used by us to examine the evolutionary trend of human society. The results show that human society also evaluate in the trend of convergence. In prehistoric times, people lived scattered in groups, later formed clans. Gradually many clans gathered together to form tribes. With increasing population, the tribal alliances, emirate, then nation in turn appeared. Entering the era of civilization, the speed of convergence is increasing. It is reflected in the urban convergence, the formation of national alliances, such as the European Union, the African Union, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations ... Besides, there are many other ways to link countries with different goals, such as the United Nations, the International Currently, humanity is facing many challenges, such as environmental issues, health issues, terrorism issues ... Therefore, social convergence is not only a law but also an urgent need. In future, the young generations are born in the flat world, will share each other the similarly living Condition and every people around the globe have convergent need. The human history is the convergent history.

results.title: Spectacle Terror Lynching, Public Sovereignty, and Antiblack Genocide
results.abstract: The history of spectacle terror lynching remains one of the darkest and least explored political events in American history. In this article, I explore the aesthetic relation of this history to the formation of notions of public action and political assembly. I argue that the history of spectacle terror lynching establishes both a past and present form of public sovereignty. As such, I attempt to examine questions of what public action means with regard to a political context of antiblack violence. I conclude that lynching festivals constitute not only a form of politics but a form of public sovereignty that is still in play in our notion of the public. At heart this notion informs not only antiblack forms of racism but antiblack forms of genocide. keywords: lynching, antiblack violence, genocide, public sovereignty, aesthetics In the short story “A Party Down at the Square,” Ralph Ellison recounts a spectacle terror lynching from the standpoint of a white observer who has never been to or heard of such an event before. The point of view that Ellison chose is striking because it is the standpoint of an outsider to lynching practices but an insider to white racial political identity. It is also striking because the observer is equally a foreigner to these scenes of violence, yet is at home with seeing violence inflicted on captive, black lynching, public sovereignty, and antiblack genocide 269 bodies. Ellison’s story complicates the narrative standpoint as it draws in notions of place and public assembly over and against the subjective reactions of the narrator, exposing several layers of entanglement. The story begins midway into the lynching of an anonymous black man, only referred to as “the nigger,” in front of a courthouse in the town square, and in doing this the story puts the space and place of the lynching into the story as a question of the sense that the public has during the lynching itself. Ellison writes: “All the wagons and cars were standing around the curbs. Not like Saturday though—the niggers weren’t there. Not a single nigger was there except this Bacote nigger and they dragged him there tied to the back of Jed Wilson’s truck. On Saturday there’s as many niggers as white folks.” He describes the place of the gathering as similar but strange, and it is strange because there are no blacks around except for the person being lynched. Ellison reinforces this sense of a collective moment in the voice of Jed Wilson: “‘What you say there, nigger?’ And it came back . . . : . . . ‘Will somebody please cut my throat like a Christian?’ And Jed hollered back, ‘Sorry, but ain’t no Christians around tonight. And no Jew-boys neither. We’re just one hundred percent Americans.’” The niggers weren’t there . . . Ain’t no Christians around tonight. . . . We’re just one hundred percent Americans. Within these lines Ellison has disclosed not only a description of America’s dark, racist past but also an aesthetic account of a political philosophy through spectacle terror lynching wedded to the question of the public, of assembly, and of violence outside of the law. The story also presents this scene as an identity point for whites—or Americans— as a moment of the construction of whiteness around racial violence and racism. But it seems to me that more is disclosed here, in that the question of the political and its limits is also presented within the feeling at home of the narrator versus the feeling of being sick—or the divergences of the aesthetic that is private from the aesthetic that is public and the entanglement of the two. I want to thematize the way aesthetic divergences are entangled with the political throughout this article as ways of animating a distinct dislocation of the political in regard to not only racial history but the specific elaboration of antiblack politics, their meaning, and their limits. I will argue throughout this article that spectacle terror lynching is distinctly an expression of not only antiblack violence, committed almost exclusively against African Americans, and predominately against men, but a much broader set of entanglements of the aesthetic and the political. Moreover, since the practices of spectacle terror lynching had alfred frankowski 270 deep ramifications for the lives of both nonwhite and white populations, they were not without political import. This warrants closer consideration, then, of how they relate to questions of politics and to sovereignty. Indeed, the problem of the sovereign goes beyond the act or the practice, though, and warrants a different set of questions other than the parameters of the political power within or outside of the nation or state. According to Jean-Jacques Rousseau, sovereignty is always mediated by the general will, or public, that gives the public political power. Along with Rousseau, Schmitt acknowledges that sovereignty is politics in a particular action that is collective. However, he warns that sovereignty is the highest power not bound by its relation to the state (or nation). It is not just the state of the public will but the action of it. Neither explicitly thematize the notion of gathering or space, and neither focus on the aesthetics of these practices as they are embedded in concrete histories, but both draw their distinctions based on not questioning the sovereignty or will that constitutes the public through its aesthetic exercises. It is this practice of mediation that traces the collisions of sovereignty. It is not clear that the historicization of lynching is not a misreading that evades the aesthetic in a particular sense of understanding and problematizing the horizon and limits of the political. If lynching is a racist action, then it is located within the political and not outside it. If it is about society’s norms or its sense of right and wrong, then it is particular, not universal. And if it is about a group, let us say the American South, and not a more general will, then it is individual. I will trace how the aesthetic problematizes these ways of framing the history of spectacle terror lynching and warrants consideration of both its aesthetic and its political import; but in doing this I will argue not only that we have misunderstood the political importance of this history and these practices as distinct forms of political praxis but that this misunderstanding has allowed us to elide the question of genocide that they so clearly illustrate. Terror Spectacle Lynching as Public Praxis In this section, I will begin by recounting three separate instances of spectacle terror lynching as acts of public aesthetics. My purpose is twofold: First, the accounts will work as context for those who may be less familiar with the structure of these events and to reinforce the aesthetic relationship lynching, public sovereignty, and antiblack genocide 271 of one to the other for those who are. Second, my goal is to illustrate the relationship these practices have to the public sense of the aesthetic through spectacle lynchings and public practices of place. All three happened in Paris, Texas, giving us a singular location for questioning this as a reproduced political activity. Each of these has been primarily reconstructed from newspaper accounts and Ida B. Wells’s anti-lynching pamphlet “A Red Record.” I have intentionally left out any reference to charges because whatever the victims of lynching were charged with is irrelevant to lynching itself and displaces the focus on both the political and the aesthetic elements of it as extrajuridical political activity. The first example is the lynching of Henry Smith, on February 1, 1893. Smith’s lynching is one of earliest spectacle terror lynchings that was documented and photographed extensively. After being arraigned for a crime that he may or may not have been guilty of, Smith—seventeen and black—was met at the train station by a mob of thousands, placed on a carnival-like float, and carried through the town to the county fairgrounds. From there he was forced onto a ten-foot-high platform, decorated with the word “JUSTICE,” and brutally beaten by representatives of the white mob for over an hour in front of a crowd numbering an estimated ten thousand people by this time. After this, he was burned slowly until his body was just a clump of charred remains. Photographers had been present before his arrival and were prepared to document the violence at every stage, from Smith’s torture to the crowd’s increased enthusiasm as his torture became more and more elaborate. The more he screamed, the more the crowd cheered. Wells wrote that “the city was wild with joy over the apprehension,” and she recounts that an onlooker who knew Smith commented that “every man, woman, and child in that awful crowd was worked up to a greater frenzy than that which actuated Smith’s crime. The people were capable of any new atrocity now, and as Smith’s yells became more frequent, it was difficult to hold the crowd back, so anxious were the savages to participate in the sickening tortures.” The second example occurred on July 6, 1920, when crowds numbering near three thousand people watched Herman and Irving Arthurs’s lynching as they were tied to a flagpole at the fairgrounds, tortured, doused with kerosene, and then slowly burned to death. In a letter to the editor of the newspaper New York Negro World, a writer pointed out that “their charred, smoking bodies were then chained to an automobile and dragged for hours through the streets, particularly in the sections inhabited by our alfred frankowski 272 Race. It was a regular parade of seventeen cars and a truck, all filled with armed men, crying aloud: ‘Here they are; two barbecued niggers. All you niggers come see them and take warning.’” The third example occurred in 2008. Brandon McClendon was found left on a roadside.
